While the football world remembers "Iron Mike" for his unparalleled competitive spirit, we admire the true character, passion, and unique energy he brought to our franchise. The best pitcher in baseball refuses to lift weights, warms up by throwing a javelin, and scouts hitters with a paper notebook. The Dodgers paid him $325 million and then hired his sensei too.

The notebook makes sense once you see the rest of his system.

Yamamoto trains under Osamu Yada, who has never told him to touch a barbell. Javelin throws instead of long toss. Handstands, back bridges, breathing work. The Dodgers studied the routine, decided they couldn't improve it, and hired Yada rather than change Yamamoto. During free agency, one team's recruiting gift to him was a team-logoed javelin, just to prove how deep their research went.

The results broke baseball's assumptions. Last November he threw 96 pitches in World Series Game 6, then came out of the bullpen and closed Game 7 the very next day.

Now look at the dugout. Every MLB club runs Hawk-Eye, a dozen cameras per stadium tracking spin, tilt, and swing path on every single pitch. Yamamoto has all of it on an iPad ten feet away.

He writes by hand anyway.

Japanese player development bakes this in. Kids keep baseball journals from little league on, charting every at-bat in their own words. The logic survives contact with analytics. League data tells you what a hitter does on average. A pitcher's own notes capture what that hitter did against him tonight, pitch by pitch, while the at-bat is still fresh. By the third time through the order, he's working from a document no analytics department can generate.

Mookie Betts watched this for two seasons. This spring he started throwing javelins too.

Baseball built the most surveilled playing field in sports. Its best October pitcher still trusts the notebook in his back pocket more.

A note from our research leaders:

Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information. Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what’s outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment. We generally keep individual employment matters private and don't believe a back and forth would be productive or lead to a resolution, but we want to address the points they raised in their letter directly.

- We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes. We have not and do not terminate any of our employees for raising concerns.

- We are actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks. People across the company have been working really hard on getting these partnerships up and running. We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively.

- We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI. Monitorability has long been a core piece of our research program, and something we continue to invest significant resources in (see our publications on Monitoring Monitorability and the subsequent open sourcing of monitorability evals, our system card for GPT-6 Astra, Jakub’s blog and post on X, and the numerous blog posts on our Alignment blog on the topic).

We are deeply sad about this outcome. We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas. We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.

DOCTORS WILL NOW GET PAID TO REPORT VACCINE INJURIES!

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a broad federal initiative focused on vaccine injuries, featuring a new research clinic at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a new medical billing code designed to reimburse doctors for reporting serious vaccine side effects. 

The program focuses on tracking and gathering data on vaccine-related adverse events through the following key components:

1. The New NIH Research Clinic
RFK Jr. established a dedicated clinic at the NIH Clinical Center in Bethesda, Maryland.

The Mission: The clinic is designed to study, evaluate, and provide care for patients who believe they have been injured by vaccines. 

Observational Studies: According to internal agency memos, the clinic will run observational studies on these patients. 

Policy Impact: RFK Jr. intends for the data gathered from this clinic to potentially inform and drive changes to the federally recommended childhood vaccine schedules. 

2. "Paying Doctors" via Medical Billing Codes
The mechanism to "pay doctors" is built around incentivizing the medical community to report suspected injuries, addressing a long-standing criticism from RFK Jr. that the current Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is inefficient because clinicians are not compensated for the time it takes to file reports.
New Billing Code: The initiative introduces a new medical billing code through Medicare/Medicaid and private insurance systems. 

Financial Reimbursement: Doctors will be able to use this code to claim financial reimbursement for the time spent documenting and filing official reports of serious or suspected vaccine side effects. 

3. Broader Policy Context
The rollout was attended by other top administration health officials, including NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz. This initiative coincides with separate plans by HHS to overhaul the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) and establish an explicit "injury table" for COVID-19 vaccines, allowing individuals with specified conditions to receive automatic government payouts.

Public Health Perspectives
Supporters argue that compensating doctors for reporting will fix a historically underreported surveillance system and offer critical help to patients suffering from rare, unaddressed medical issues.

Mainstream public health experts express significant worry that the initiative could validate scientifically unproven claims (such as linking vaccines to autism or widespread allergies), overwhelm the medical system with unverified reports, and inadvertently fuel vaccine hesitancy amid rising outbreaks of preventable diseases.
